meta.title: Statistics
meta.source_edition: NCERT Reprint 2026-27, Class 10 Mathematics, Ch 13 (jemh113.pdf, printed pages 171-201)

board_asks: the mean of grouped data (direct, assumed-mean, step-deviation), the mode of grouped data, and the median of grouped data via a cumulative-frequency table & class marks — plus the reverse question “the median is given, find the missing frequency”. Almost every mark here is a plug-into-the-formula computation, so identifying the right class (modal / median) and reading off $l, f, cf, h$ correctly is where the marks live.

big_idea.body: In Class IX you found the mean, median and mode of ungrouped data. This chapter extends all three measures of central tendency to grouped data — data bundled into class intervals like $40{-}55$. Because you no longer see individual observations, each method works on a representative of the class: the class mark (mid-point) for the mean, the modal class for the mode, and the median class (located with cumulative frequencies) for the median. Learn to spot the right class and substitute into the right formula, and every question in this chapter falls out.

definitions.verbatim: The mean (or average) of observations, as we know, is the sum of the values of all the observations divided by the total number of observations.
definitions.plain: for grouped data you cannot see each value, so you use the class mark $x_i$ of each class as its stand-in: $\bar{x} = \dfrac{\Sigma f_i x_i}{\Sigma f_i}$.

definitions.verbatim: It is assumed that the frequency of each class-interval is centred around its mid-point. So the mid-point (or class mark) of each class can be chosen to represent the observations falling in the class.
definitions.plain: $\text{class mark} = \dfrac{\text{upper limit} + \text{lower limit}}{2}$. This single number represents the whole class in the mean calculation — it is your $x_i$.

definitions.verbatim: Recall from Class IX, a mode is that value among the observations which occurs most often, that is, the value of the observation having the maximum frequency.
definitions.plain: the most-frequent value. For grouped data you cannot read it off directly — you locate the modal class (the class with the greatest frequency) and use the mode formula.

definitions.verbatim: the median is a measure of central tendency which gives the value of the middle-most observation in the data.
definitions.plain: the middle value once the data is ordered. For grouped data the middle observation sits inside a class, so you find the median class using cumulative frequencies and the median formula.

definitions.verbatim: In a grouped frequency distribution, it is not possible to determine the mode by looking at the frequencies. Here, we can only locate a class with the maximum frequency, called the modal class.
definitions.plain: the class interval with the highest frequency. Its lower limit $l$ and the frequencies $f_1$ (modal), $f_0$ (preceding), $f_2$ (succeeding) feed the mode formula.

definitions.verbatim: This new method of finding the mean is known as the Direct Method.
The method discussed above is called the Assumed Mean Method.
the step-deviation method will be convenient to apply if all the di's have a common factor.

source.note: companion statement on p.177: "The method discussed above is called the Step-deviation method."; "di's" is NCERT's own notation for the deviations, preserved verbatim

definitions.verbatim: We now locate the class whose cumulative frequency is greater than (and nearest to) [n/2] This is called the median class.

source.note: the 2D-typeset fraction n/2 is bracketed as an editorial insert; both prose runs are verbatim on p.193

definitions.verbatim: The cumulative frequency of a class is the frequency obtained by adding the frequencies of all the classes preceding the given class.
There is a empirical relationship between the three measures of central tendency : [3 Median = Mode + 2 Mean]

source.note: NCERT Remark, p.197; "a empirical" is NCERT's own wording, preserved verbatim; the formula 3 Median = Mode + 2 Mean is bracketed as an editorial insert

concepts.title: Mean of grouped data — three methods, same answer
concepts.body: Replace each class by its class mark $x_i$, then use whichever method keeps the arithmetic small: Direct $\bar{x}=\dfrac{\Sigma f_i x_i}{\Sigma f_i}$ · Assumed-mean $\bar{x}=a+\dfrac{\Sigma f_i d_i}{\Sigma f_i}$ (with $d_i=x_i-a$) · Step-deviation $\bar{x}=a+h\!\left(\dfrac{\Sigma f_i u_i}{\Sigma f_i}\right)$ (with $u_i=\dfrac{x_i-a}{h}$). All three give the identical mean — step-deviation is fastest when the $d_i$ share a common factor $h$.
concepts.tested: 3-mark “find the mean of the following distribution” — a fixture of every board paper

concepts.title: Mode of grouped data — find the modal class first
concepts.body: Spot the modal class (highest frequency), read off $l$ (its lower limit), $h$ (class size), $f_1$ (modal frequency), $f_0$ (preceding), $f_2$ (succeeding), then $\text{Mode}=l+\left(\dfrac{f_1-f_0}{2f_1-f_0-f_2}\right)h$. The commonest slip is a sign error in the denominator $2f_1-f_0-f_2$.
concepts.tested: 3-mark “find the mode”, often paired with “compare and interpret the mode and the mean”

concepts.title: Median of grouped data — locate the median class via cumulative frequency
concepts.body: Build the cumulative frequency column, compute $\dfrac{n}{2}$, and pick the median class — the first class whose cumulative frequency is $\ge \dfrac{n}{2}$. Then $\text{Median}=l+\left(\dfrac{\frac{n}{2}-cf}{f}\right)h$, where $cf$ is the cumulative frequency of the class preceding the median class. Watch: $cf$ is from the class before, not the median class itself.
concepts.tested: 3-mark “find the median”, and the reverse 5-mark “median given, find the missing frequency”

concepts.title: Which measure, and the empirical bridge
concepts.body: Mean uses every observation but is dragged by extreme values; median resists extremes (best for ‘typical’ wage/productivity); mode answers ‘most popular / most frequent’. When two are known, the empirical relation $3\,\text{Median}=\text{Mode}+2\,\text{Mean}$ estimates the third. ⚑ Syllabus note (2026-27): the graphical method of finding the median is OUT of the rationalised syllabus — here the median is computed by formula only, from a cumulative-frequency table.
concepts.tested: “compare and interpret the two measures” parts; estimate-the-third using $3\,\text{Median}=\text{Mode}+2\,\text{Mean}$

examples.shape: Mean by all three methods · NCERT Example 2
examples.problem_verbatim: The table below gives the percentage distribution of female teachers in the primary schools of rural areas of various states and union territories (U.T.) of India. Find the mean percentage of female teachers by all the three methods discussed in this section.

solution_steps.lead: Set up class marks and totals.
solution_steps.text: Class marks $x_i = 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80$ with frequencies $f_i = 6, 11, 7, 4, 4, 2, 1$. Taking $a = 50$, $h = 10$: $\Sigma f_i = 35$, $\Sigma f_i x_i = 1390$, $\Sigma f_i d_i = -360$, $\Sigma f_i u_i = -36$.
$\bar{x} = a + \dfrac{\Sigma f_i d_i}{\Sigma f_i} = 50 + \dfrac{-360}{35} = 39.71$ — same answer.
$\bar{x} = a + h\!\left(\dfrac{\Sigma f_i u_i}{\Sigma f_i}\right) = 50 + 10\times\dfrac{-36}{35} = 39.71$. So the mean percentage of female teachers is $39.71$.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark shape: 1 for the class-mark table and column sums, 1 for computing the mean by one method, 1 shared for confirming the other two methods give the identical 39.71. NCERT's point is that the choice of method is a convenience, not a different answer.

source.note: problem on p.178, worked table + all three methods on p.179

examples.shape: Step-deviation with unequal classes · NCERT Example 3
examples.problem_verbatim: The distribution below shows the number of wickets taken by bowlers in one-day cricket matches. Find the mean number of wickets by choosing a suitable method. What does the mean signify?

solution_steps.lead: Choose the step-deviation method (classes are unequal, $x_i$ large).

solution_steps.text: $\bar{x} = 200 + \dfrac{-106}{45}\times 20 = 200 - 47.11 = 152.89$. This tells us that, on average, these 45 bowlers took about 153 wickets each in one-day cricket.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark shape: 1 for choosing step-deviation and building the $u_i$ column, 1 for $\Sigma f_i u_i = -106$, 1 for $\bar{x} = 152.89$ with the interpretation. The step-deviation method still works with unequal classes when a suitable $h$ divides the $d_i$.

examples.shape: Mode of grouped data · NCERT Example 5
examples.problem_verbatim: A survey conducted on 20 households in a locality by a group of students resulted in the following frequency table for the number of family members in a household: ... Find the mode of this data.

solution_steps.text: The maximum frequency is 8, in the class $3-5$, so the modal class is $3-5$: $l = 3$, $h = 2$, $f_1 = 8$, $f_0 = 7$ (class before), $f_2 = 2$ (class after).
$= 3 + \dfrac{1}{7}\times 2 = 3.286$. So the mode of the data is $3.286$.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark shape: 1 for identifying the modal class $3-5$ and reading off $l, h, f_1, f_0, f_2$, 1 for correct substitution into the mode formula, 1 for the value $3.286$. The classic lost mark is a sign slip in the denominator $2f_1 - f_0 - f_2$.

source.note: problem stem on p.183, solution on p.184-185; the frequency table is elided ("...") and acknowledged non-verbatim

examples.shape: Median from a less-than table · NCERT Example 7
examples.problem_verbatim: A survey regarding the heights (in cm) of 51 girls of Class X of a school was conducted and the following data was obtained: ... Find the median height.

solution_steps.lead: Convert less-than data to class frequencies + cumulative frequency.
solution_steps.text: Classes below 140, 140-145, 145-150, 150-155, 155-160, 160-165 have frequencies $4, 7, 18, 11, 6, 5$, with cumulative frequencies $4, 11, 29, 40, 46, 51$.
$n = 51$, so $\dfrac{n}{2} = 25.5$. The class $145-150$ is the first with cumulative frequency $(29) \ge 25.5$, so it is the median class: $l = 145$, $cf = 11$ (preceding class), $f = 18$, $h = 5$.
$\text{Median} = l + \left(\dfrac{\frac{n}{2} - cf}{f}\right)h = 145 + \left(\dfrac{25.5 - 11}{18}\right)\times 5 = 145 + \dfrac{72.5}{18} = 149.03$. So the median height is $149.03$ cm.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark shape: 1 for turning the less-than table into class frequencies and cumulative frequencies, 1 for locating the median class $145-150$ and reading off $l, cf, f, h$, 1 for the value $149.03$ cm. $cf$ must be the cumulative frequency of the class BEFORE the median class.

source.note: problem on p.194, solution on p.194-195; the less-than data table is elided ("...") and acknowledged non-verbatim

examples.shape: Reverse: median given, find missing frequencies · NCERT Example 8
examples.problem_verbatim: The median of the following data is 525. Find the values of x and y, if the total frequency is 100.

solution_steps.lead: Write the cumulative frequency column in terms of x and y.

solution_steps.text: Median $= 525$ lies in the class $500-600$, so $l = 500$, $f = 20$, $cf = 36 + x$, $h = 100$, and $\dfrac{n}{2} = 50$.

solution_steps.lead: Substitute into the median formula and solve for x.

solution_steps.text: From Equation 1: $9 + y = 24 \Rightarrow y = 15$. So $x = 9$ and $y = 15$.

examples.mark_logic: 5-mark shape: 1 for the cumulative-frequency column in $x, y$ · 1 for $x + y = 24$ from the total · 1 for locating the median class $500-600$ and reading $l, f, cf, h$ · 1 for substituting into the median formula and solving $x = 9$ · 1 for $y = 15$. Miss the total-frequency equation and you cannot close for both unknowns.

source.note: problem on p.195, solution on p.195-196

strategies.text: Write class marks $x_i$, then pick the lightest arithmetic: direct if $x_i, f_i$ small; assumed-mean / step-deviation if they are large or the $d_i$ share a common factor $h$.
Circle the modal class (max frequency), read off $l, h, f_1, f_0, f_2$, then $\text{Mode}=l+\left(\dfrac{f_1-f_0}{2f_1-f_0-f_2}\right)h$.
Build the cumulative frequency column, compute $\frac{n}{2}$, locate the median class (first $cf \ge \frac{n}{2}$), then plug $l, cf, f, h$ into the median formula.
Convert to continuous classes (117.5-126.5, 126.5-135.5, ...) BEFORE applying the mode or median formula.
Set up the cumulative frequency column with the unknowns, use $n$ for one equation and the median formula for another, then solve the pair.

pitfalls.text: $cf$ is the cumulative frequency of the class PRECEDING the median class — not of the median class itself. Reading the wrong row is the commonest median error.
Not converting to continuous classes before the mode/median formula (e.g. 118-126 must become 117.5-126.5) — the formulae assume continuous intervals.
Sign slip in the mode denominator $2f_1 - f_0 - f_2$ — subtract BOTH $f_0$ and $f_2$.
Picking the wrong class — the modal class is the one with the maximum frequency; the median class is the first whose cumulative frequency reaches $\frac{n}{2}$. Confusing the two wrecks the answer.

third_tab_content.name: Why the assumed-mean & step-deviation formulas work
third_tab_content.intro: NCERT derives the assumed-mean and step-deviation formulas from the direct method (pp.174-177) — they are just simplified forms that shrink the arithmetic, not different definitions of the mean. Following the derivation shows WHY the mean comes out identical whichever method you choose, and why any convenient $a$ and $h$ work.

steps.claim: Pick an assumed mean $a$ (a convenient class mark) and take the deviation of each class mark from it.
Define the mean of the deviations.
Substitute $d_i = x_i - a$ and split the sum — $a$ is constant, so it factors out.
steps.math: $\bar{d} = \dfrac{\Sigma f_i (x_i - a)}{\Sigma f_i} = \dfrac{\Sigma f_i x_i}{\Sigma f_i} - a = \bar{x} - a$
steps.justification: $\dfrac{\Sigma f_i x_i}{\Sigma f_i}$ is exactly the direct-method mean $\bar{x}$, and $\dfrac{a\,\Sigma f_i}{\Sigma f_i}=a$.

steps.claim: Rearrange to get the Assumed Mean Method.
To shrink the numbers further, scale the deviations by the class size $h$.
Rearrange to get the Step-deviation Method — and note $a, h$ may be any convenient numbers.
steps.math: $\bar{x} = a + h\,\bar{u} = a + h\!\left(\dfrac{\Sigma f_i u_i}{\Sigma f_i}\right)$
steps.justification: The formula still holds for any non-zero $h$, so you choose $a$ and $h$ to make the columns small — that is the whole point of the method.

source.note: derivation runs across pp.174-177 (assumed-mean relation d̄ = x̄ − a on p.175; step-deviation relation x̄ = a + h·ū on pp.176-177)
